@data.description: A component's data target: repositories, clients, stores, DTOs.

@host.description: A DI container. Hosts wire concrete types; features must depend on ports instead.

@port.description: Cross-cutting UI ports — a protocol a feature calls, whose host is linked only by the composition root.

@domain.description: Component domain targets. A target missing from this list is not judged leniently — it is not judged at all: no layer's deny of @domain catches importing it, so every Component/*/Sources/Domain target must be named here.

@library.description: No domain knowledge; depended on by anyone.

@infrastructure.description: Modules that exist only to reach something outside the process. Denying this group is how the domain and the screens are kept off storage — but it can only deny whole modules, and this project's actual persistence is Foundation: FileManager, Data.write, UserDefaults. Foundation cannot be listed here, because URL, Date and UUID are legitimately everywhere. So this group alone promises more containment than it delivers, and persistence-stays-behind-a-gateway carries the rest by name instead.

composition-root.description: The one place that knows every concrete type. Wiring only.

library.description: Domain-free utilities. Money and Networking know nothing about this app.

imports.reason: A Library/ module must stay ignorant of the app that links it. If it needs a domain type, it is not a library — move it into the component that owns the concept.

domain.description: Entities, use cases and repository contracts. The stable core.

imports.reason: Domain declares protocols; infrastructure implements them. Declare the contract in Sources/Domain/Repository/ and put the implementation in Sources/Data/ — then wire the conformance in Sources/DI/. Source code dependencies must point only inward.
notes: Combine is deliberate and load-bearing: the architecture is reactive, and the domain publishes change rather than being polled for it. Do not remove it in the name of framework purity.
@domain is allowed because a domain may depend on and execute another domain and its use cases. Wishlist requiring a Session, and a use case composing other use cases, are business rules — not leaks.

A component is not required to have a Data target. Home has none and should not be given one: its feed is derived from Product's use cases on every draw, never stored, so there is no contract for a repository to satisfy. Its container is still built in DomainAssembler with the others — a component container belongs to the second phase whether or not it needs a store.

data.description: Implements domain contracts. Knows networking, persistence and hashing.

imports.reason: The data layer answers to the domain, never to a screen. If a repository needs something from the UI, the dependency is inverted — pass it in from the composition root instead.

component-di.description: A component's container: the only place its domain meets its data.

imports.reason: A component container wires domain to data. It has no business knowing which screens exist.

presentation.description: Views and ViewModels. Views are passive; ViewModels delegate to use cases.

imports.reason: UI reaches the domain, never storage, and depends on ports rather than hosts. Inject the use case protocol through the initialiser and let Sources/DI/ decide the concrete type. Importing a @host here links a whole dependency graph into a screen that only needed one protocol.

ui-port.description: A cross-cutting UI port: the protocol a feature calls, with no implementation behind it here.

imports.reason: A port is the interface, declared where it is used. It must not reach a host, a data target or infrastructure — that is what makes it substitutable.

ui-port-host.description: The implementation behind a port. Linked only by the composition root.

imports.reason: A host builds and presents the port's UI. It reaches a component through that component's container, never into its data target.

ui-port-di.description: A port's container: the one place the port meets its host.

feature-navigation.description: A feature's navigation protocol — what it can ask for, not who answers.

imports.reason: Navigation declares intent as a protocol. The composition root supplies the implementation.

feature-di.description: A feature's container. May take peer containers to build child views.

imports.reason: A feature container composes views and use cases. It reaches a component through that component's container, never into its data target.

tests.description: A package's two test tiers: an acceptance suite driven through a testing API in the shopper's language, and a unit suite in the language of the system.

structure.name: use-cases-live-in-domain
structure.reason: A use case is application-specific business logic. It belongs in Sources/Domain/UseCases/, not beside a view or a repository. A test may declare one: standing in for a collaborator is what a test double is for, and the unit tier writes them in the language of the system.

structure.name: repository-contracts-live-in-domain
structure.reason: The contract belongs to the domain; only the implementation belongs to data.

structure.name: repository-implementations-live-in-data
structure.reason: A concrete repository is infrastructure. Put it in Sources/Data/ and let Sources/DI/ hand it to the domain as its protocol.

structure.name: dtos-live-in-data
structure.reason: A DTO is a wire-format concern. It must not escape the data layer — map it to a domain type at the boundary.

structure.name: view-models-live-in-presentation
structure.reason: ViewModels are presentation. A ViewModel outside a UI target means business logic has followed it there.

structure.name: screens-map-domain-types-rather-than-extending-them
structure.reason: A UI module may not add members to a domain type. An extension gives one type a different surface depending on which module is reading it — a member exists on Order in the package that declared it and silently does not in the package next door, which grows its own copy of the same rule instead. Build a presentation model: a struct of already-worded values, mapped from the domain type by an init in its own body. Wording belongs to the screen, so pre-word it there and let the view move data into the GUI without processing it. Extending a type a UI module owns, or a domain type inside a test fixture, is fine. The names are a roster, not a computed set: a regex cannot ask which types a Component/*/Sources/Domain target declares, so what is listed is the type each component hands across the boundary — the aggregate root, and where a root is a collection of a second published type, that type too. Home publishes both HomeFeed and the HomeCarousel a view binds to, so both are named; a component whose root is the only type UI receives needs one name. Settings hands over four: the Settings record, the SettingKey a row is identified by and a toggle hands back, the SettingsSection a section is identified by, and the Setting — one key and its value — that ObserveOfferedSettingsUseCase actually publishes and the screen actually receives. SettingKey and SettingsSection are named because the screen's two wording tables are keyed on exactly them; a title on either is the extension somebody would otherwise write. Setting is named because it is what now crosses the boundary, and an isOn-plus-title extension on it is the shortest path back to putting wording on a domain type. The four are ordered longest-first in the alternation on purpose: Setting is a strict prefix of the other three, and an engine that takes the first alternative rather than the longest could match Setting inside Settings, fail the trailing \b and let a real violation through. Ordering removes the question. Each of the four was probed against the built rule after the change, not reasoned about. Known debt, recorded so it is not rediscovered and re-filed: the roster is narrower than the criterion it states. BagItem, ProductCategory, OrderLine, Notices, Availability, CatalogFilter, CatalogQuery and SearchTerm all cross into a UI module today and none is named, so an extension on any of them would go uncaught — note that \bBag\b does not match BagItem, which is the trap here, since Bag is rostered and the item a row actually binds to is not. Nothing violates it now; every one of those types was checked and none is extended anywhere under UI/. Closing it means widening the roster across nine packages and is deliberately not folded into whichever feature notices it next.

structure.name: tests-belong-to-one-of-the-two-tiers
structure.reason: A test file belongs to one of two tiers: an acceptance suite driven through a testing API, or a unit suite driven through the seams of the code. A new behaviour is a new journey on an existing driver or a new case in an existing unit suite — not a new target.

structure.name: acceptance-tests-speak-the-shoppers-language
structure.reason: No acceptance test may name a repository, store, DTO or Default*UseCase. Drive the feature through its testing API — Shopper, Shop, Account, Saver, Searcher — so the feature can be rearranged underneath the suite without touching it. Support/ files and the unit tier may name concrete types; the acceptance suite may not.

structure.name: persistence-stays-behind-a-gateway
structure.reason: A screen, a domain and a library may not touch the file system or the user defaults directly. Put it behind a store in Sources/Data/ and let the domain hold the protocol. This exists because the @infrastructure group cannot do it: denying a module catches CoreData and SwiftData, but this project persists through Foundation, and Foundation is allow-listed everywhere because URL and Date are not storage. Naming the four types closes that gap where it actually leaks. iPhone/ is deliberately not matched — choosing UserDefaults.standard is the composition root's whole job. Component/*/Sources/Data/ is not matched either, because that is where these types belong.

structure.name: no-todo-comments
structure.reason: Do the work or delete the code. A tracked issue outlives a comment nobody reads.

manifests.name: domain-target-stays-pure
manifests.reason: A component's domain target may not gain a Data, UI or DI dependency. Package.swift is what makes the dependency rule real — the compiler enforces it only because this file says so. If the domain needs something, invert it: declare a protocol in Sources/Domain/Repository/ and satisfy it from Sources/Data/.

manifests.name: components-take-no-third-party-dependencies
manifests.reason: Domain and data stay first-party. A third-party package in a component is a volatile dependency pointing at the stable core — put the adapter in Library/ behind a protocol instead.

manifests.name: no-test-target-beyond-the-two-tiers
manifests.reason: A package declares at most two test targets: one acceptance suite and one unit suite. A third test target is a layer test in disguise.

tiers.name: unit
tiers.reason: Every component needs a unit tier: tests written by programmers, in the language of the system, naming the unit that broke. An acceptance failure says checkout is broken; a unit failure says which rule is wrong. Required of Component/* and deliberately not of UI/*: a UI package earns a unit tier by having a ViewModel, and OnboardingUI, SheetUI and SnackbarUI have none, so requiring one of every UI/* would demand a suite for nothing. requiredFor takes path globs alone, so "a UI package with a ViewModel needs a unit tier" cannot be stated here, and naming the ones that qualify would be a roster that goes stale rather than a rule. This sentence used to carry that count and had to be re-incremented by every task that added a package — a number that is wrong the moment nobody remembers to bump it, which is how a manifest drifts out of date while still reading as precise. So the standard is stated without one: every UI package that has a ViewModel has a unit tier, and that is checked in review, not here.

tiers.name: acceptance
tiers.reason: Every component needs an acceptance tier stating its business rules as a journey a person takes, readable by someone who does not know the code. Required of Component/* and deliberately not of UI/*, for the same mechanical reason the unit tier gives: requiredFor takes path globs alone, so "a UI package a shopper drives" cannot be stated here, and OnboardingUI, SheetUI and SnackbarUI would be made to invent a journey for a view that has no behaviour. Unlike the unit tier, the UI side of this one is not yet whole, and saying so here is the point of this sentence: BagUI, HomeUI, OrderUI, ProductActionsUI, SettingsUI and WishlistUI have an acceptance tier; AccountUI, AuthUI, ProductUI and SearchUI do not. AccountUI, AuthUI and SearchUI own journeys worth stating and are real debt. ProductUI is the weakest of the four — it is the shared view kit (card, row, grid) plus one thin details view model — and is not in violation of this rule. Recorded so the gap is known rather than rediscovered and re-filed.

notes: Property testing: ruled out, re-argued against the rule that now exists. This entry previously reasoned from categories.shuffled().prefix(3), which DrawHomeFeedUseCase no longer does; the conclusion survived the rewrite but the reason had to be replaced rather than kept. Home now shuffles the shop's categories once and walks them front to back, trying each at most once, taking a carousel from any category with at least 5 products, showing at most 10 of them, and stopping at 5 carousels. Its invariants are: between 1 and 5 carousels on success, all distinct, all the shop's own categories, each holding 5 to 10 products, and failure exactly when none qualified. They still do not earn a generator, because the outcome turns on one number — how many of the shop's categories clear the floor — and equals min(that, 5), failing only at zero. The boundaries of a one-variable function are 0, 1, 5 and 6, and the suites already name every one of them; the per-carousel size is a second such variable, pinned at 0, 4, 5, 6, 10 and 15. Distinctness and "all real" remain properties of walking a shuffled array once, which is the Swift standard library's behaviour and not a rule this project owns. Against that stands the cost, unchanged: a generator framework would be the second third-party package in the entire graph after Kingfisher, in a repository whose purpose is to be read, and a reader would have to learn the framework before they could read the tests that demonstrate the architecture. Do not reopen without a rule whose input space genuinely cannot be enumerated.

Test doubles and fixtures are duplicated between each package's two Tests/*/Support/ files. That is forced by the tiers being separate targets and no-test-target-beyond-the-two-tiers forbidding a third to share them, and it is wanted: the acceptance tier's doubles are a shop, the unit tier's are stubs, and they should be free to drift apart. Not duplication to remove.

Some acceptance tiers drive through their testing API but observe around it. A testing API with verbs for arranging the world — sells, opensHome — and none for seeing it leaves the tests asserting on the view model's published properties, so renaming a published property breaks an acceptance suite that no shopper would notice had changed. That is the Fragile Tests Problem the testing API exists to prevent: "The role of the testing API is to hide the structure of the application from the tests" (Martin, Clean Architecture, Ch. 28 — The Test Boundary; the passage was checked in the library). Where it still bites: BagUIAcceptanceTests asserts on viewModel.notices, viewModel.rows, viewModel.total and viewModel.isEmpty, and WishlistUIAcceptanceTests reaches through AKeeper to keeper.list.products, keeper.list.savedCount and keeper.list.isEmpty. OrderUI and ProductActionsUI read a double's own record rather than a view model's published state, which is weaker coupling but still not a verb. HomeUI — which this entry once cited as the worst case, at 25 assertions — now is one: its twelve assertions go through carouselsShown, isOfferedAnotherGo and drawAttempts, and it is the closest thing here to a worked example. acceptance-tests-speak-the-shoppers-language catches only the names of repositories, stores, DTOs and Default*UseCases; no regex separates reading a view model's state from a legitimate call on the testing API, so this is not made a rule and is recorded as a review point instead. The measure of a fix: a change to how a screen holds its state should touch no acceptance test. What a testing API may hand back, settled when SettingsUI declined to copy HomeUI and the break was ratified rather than corrected: a domain type, yes; a presentation model the package itself owns, no. HomeUI's carouselsShown hands back HomeCarousel, which changes only when the business changes — and an acceptance suite is supposed to break when the business changes. SettingsUI's sections would have handed back SettingsSectionModel, which changes when somebody reshapes the screen, and that is precisely the move the measure above says must touch no acceptance test. So SettingsUI answers instead in sectionsShown: [String], rowsShown(in section: String) -> [String] and isOn(_ key:) -> Bool?, and its acceptance tier names neither SettingsSectionModel nor SettingRow. The middle one is asked a section at a time rather than flat on purpose: which section a row sits under is part of what a shopper sees, and one flat list of every row reads identically however the rows are grouped, so a flat accessor would have let a mis-grouping through unnoticed. This is not a third style competing with HomeUI's; it is the same measure reaching a different answer because the state in question is the package's own. "The goal is to decouple the structure of the tests from the structure of the application", and "Structural coupling is one of the strongest, and most insidious, forms of test coupling" (Martin, Clean Architecture, Ch. 28 — The Test Boundary; both passages were checked in the library). A presentation model is the structure of the application. A domain type is the structure of the business. Hand back the second, never the first.

HomeUI's two tiers now stub the same collaborator — DrawHomeFeedUseCase — and drive the same object; the rest fake a repository in the acceptance tier and use cases in the unit tier. Reviewed and kept. Once the feed rule moved to Component/Home, everything left in HomeUI is the screen's own: what it shows while loading, what it shows when nothing could be drawn, that it does not redraw on a second appearance, and where a tap goes. There is no lower seam left to fake. Wiring the real use case back in would drag Component/Home's floor of 5 into a suite about a screen, so a change to that rule would break tests that are not about it — the fragile coupling the entry above is about, reintroduced deliberately. What separates the two tiers is no longer the seam but what breaks them: the acceptance tier speaks in journeys and survives a change to how the screen holds state, the unit tier names state, .loading and callCount and is meant not to. Component/Home's own acceptance tier still runs Product's real use cases against a fake shop, so the integration that HomeUI gave up is still tested, one package down. SettingsUI looked at first like the same shape and turned out not to be, and the difference is the point, so it is settled here rather than left for review. Both its tiers do stub the same collaborator — ObserveOfferedSettingsUseCase and SetSettingUseCase, driving SettingsScreenViewModel. But its acceptance tier's stub is not a canned answer the way StubDrawHomeFeed is: it fakes only what the shop says — a settings record, whether the shopper is signed in, and a write that keeps what it is given — and then calls the real Setting.offered(from:signedIn:) in Component/Settings, the same call the app makes. So the rule that decides which settings a shopper has is genuinely under test one layer up, which is what makes the sign-in and sign-out-while-the-screen-is-open journeys mean anything; had the driver re-decided availability itself, those two would have been asserting on the test's own arithmetic. The general form: stubbing a use case in both tiers is acceptable when there is no lower seam left, and is better still when the acceptance tier fakes the inputs to a domain rule rather than its output. HomeUI does the first. SettingsUI does the second and is the better example to copy.
